Under s.205 the Company Secretary reports to the board on compliance with the Act and rules, ensures compliance with secretarial standards, and discharges other prescribed duties. In practice the CS drafts notices and agenda, ensures quorum, records proceedings, maintains statutory registers and files forms. The CS also guides directors on their duties and facilitates board evaluation.

Secretarial Standard on Meetings of the Board (SS-1) is mandatory under s.118(10) and applies to board and committee meetings. It requires, among other things, serial numbering of meetings, attendance register, circulation of draft minutes within 15 days for comments within 7 days, and entry of minutes in the minute book within 30 days. It also prescribes conditions for meetings through video conferencing and for resolution by circulation.

A board notice should give serial number, date, day, time, venue and VC option, and be accompanied by the agenda and notes with draft resolutions. Minutes should record the names of directors present, the chairman, leave of absence, items discussed in brief, decisions and dissent, and must be signed by the chairman at the next meeting or within 30 days. Example operative text: 'RESOLVED THAT the unaudited financial results for the quarter ended ... be and are hereby approved'.

quiz.q: A company has 8 directors. The quorum for its board meeting is:
quiz.explain: Section 174(1) requires one-third of total strength (8/3 rounded up = 3) or two, whichever higher.

quiz.q: A board meeting was held on 1 January. The next must be held no later than:
quiz.explain: Section 173(1) limits the gap between two meetings to 120 days.

quiz.q: Draft minutes of a board meeting must be circulated to directors within:
quiz.explain: SS-1 requires circulation of draft minutes within 15 days of the meeting.

quiz.q: A resolution by circulation is sent to 9 directors; 3 directors require it to be decided at a meeting. Result:
options: It is passed if majority approve
The chairman must put it to a board meeting
quiz.explain: Section 175(1) proviso requires a meeting where one-third or more directors so demand.

quiz.q: Which item can NOT be approved by circulation?
quiz.explain: Section 179(3) powers, including approval of financial statements, must be exercised at a meeting.

quiz.q: A board meeting is called at short notice for urgent business. No independent director attends. The decision is:
options: Final only if ratified by at least one independent director
quiz.explain: Section 173(3) proviso requires circulation and ratification by an independent director in such cases.

desc.q: As CS of Nova Ltd, you must convene a board meeting to approve the quarterly results and a proposed investment in a subsidiary. Prepare the essential steps from notice to minutes.
points: Issue notice with serial number, date, time, venue and VC option at least 7 days in advance to all directors (s.173(3)), and intimate stock exchanges where required under LODR.
Circulate agenda with notes and draft resolutions at least 7 days before (SS-1); results may be circulated at shorter notice as UPSI with required consent.
Ensure quorum under s.174 and record attendance; the investment under s.186 needs unanimous approval of directors present.
Record proceedings, decisions and dissent; circulate draft minutes within 15 days for comments within 7 days.
Sign minutes within 30 days and file MGT-14 where required; disclose outcome to stock exchanges within the prescribed time.

notes.note: Section 135 applies to companies with net worth of ₹500 crore, turnover of ₹1,000 crore or net profit of ₹5 crore in the preceding financial year. They constitute a CSR Committee of three or more directors including at least one independent director; a company not required to appoint an independent director need not have one, and a private company with only two directors may have a two-member committee. If the CSR obligation does not exceed ₹50 lakh, the board itself can discharge the committee's functions.

The CSR Committee formulates and recommends a CSR policy and an annual action plan covering projects, execution modalities, fund allocation, monitoring and impact assessment. The board approves the policy and discloses its contents in the board's report and on the website. The policy should exclude activities in the normal course of business and those benefiting only employees.

The company must spend at least 2% of average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years on CSR. Unspent amounts not relating to ongoing projects must be transferred to a Schedule VII fund within six months of year-end; excess spend can be set off over the next three years. Administrative overheads are capped at 5% of total CSR expenditure, and surplus from CSR activities cannot become business profit.

Activities must fall within Schedule VII, such as eradicating hunger, promoting education, gender equality, environmental sustainability, rural development, disaster management and contributions to specified funds like PM CARES. Implementation can be direct, through a section 8 company, registered trust or society with CSR-1 registration, or in collaboration. Activities only for employees, political contributions and one-off sponsorship events for marketing do not count.

An ongoing project is a multi-year project with a timeline not exceeding three years excluding the year of commencement. Unspent amounts for ongoing projects are transferred to an Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of year-end and spent within three financial years, after which any balance goes to a Schedule VII fund within 30 days. This allows long-term projects such as building a school without immediate lapse.

Companies with an average CSR obligation of ₹10 crore or more in the three preceding years must undertake impact assessment through an independent agency for projects of ₹1 crore or more completed at least a year ago. The report is placed before the board and annexed to the annual CSR report. Expenditure on impact assessment can be booked as CSR within the higher of 2% of the year's CSR spend or ₹50 lakh.

quiz.q: A company had a net profit of ₹6 crore in the preceding year but turnover and net worth below thresholds. CSR is:
quiz.explain: Section 135(1) applies if any one criterion, including net profit of ₹5 crore, is met.

quiz.q: A company's CSR obligation is ₹40 lakh. Must it constitute a CSR Committee?
options: No, the board can perform its functions
quiz.explain: Section 135(9) exempts a committee where the amount does not exceed ₹50 lakh.

quiz.q: Unspent CSR for an ongoing project must be transferred to the Unspent CSR Account within:
options: 30 days of the end of the financial year
quiz.explain: Section 135(6) requires transfer within 30 days from the end of the financial year.

quiz.q: Which activity is eligible for CSR?
options: Sponsoring a marketing event for the company's brand
Building a school in a rural district
quiz.explain: Promoting education is a Schedule VII activity; employee-only and political spends are excluded.

quiz.q: The cap on administrative overheads in CSR spending is:
quiz.explain: Rule 7 of CSR Rules limits administrative overheads to 5% of total CSR expenditure.

quiz.q: Impact assessment is mandatory for a company with average CSR obligation of at least:
quiz.explain: Rule 8(3) of CSR Rules applies to companies with average CSR obligation of ₹10 crore or more.

desc.q: Pi Ltd's CSR obligation for FY 2026-27 is ₹3 crore. It spent ₹1.5 crore; ₹1 crore is committed to a three-year ongoing school project and ₹0.5 crore is simply unspent. Advise on the treatment and disclosure.
points: CSR obligation is 2% of average net profits of the three preceding years under s.135(5).
₹1 crore for the ongoing project must go to an Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of year-end and be spent within three years (s.135(6)).
The other ₹0.5 crore not linked to an ongoing project must be transferred to a Schedule VII fund within six months of year-end (s.135(5) proviso).
Board's report must disclose the CSR policy, annual report on CSR activities, and reasons for unspent amounts.
Non-compliance attracts penalty on the company (twice the unspent amount or ₹1 crore, whichever is less) and on officers in default.

notes.note: Under s.134(3) the board's report covers matters such as the web link of the annual return, number of board meetings, directors' responsibility statement, statement on independent directors' declarations, policy on appointment and remuneration, explanations on auditor qualifications, loans and investments, RPTs (AOC-2), state of affairs, dividend, reserves, material changes, energy conservation and CSR. It is approved by the board and signed by the chairperson if authorised, or by at least two directors including the MD. One Person Companies and small companies get an abridged format under rule 8A.

Under s.92 every company files an annual return in MGT-7 (MGT-7A for OPCs and small companies) within 60 days of the AGM, with details of registered office, business, shareholding, members, directors, KMP, meetings and remuneration. A listed company or one with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or turnover of ₹50 crore needs certification by a practising CS in MGT-8. The return must also be placed on the company's website, if it has one.

The annual report bundles the financial statements, auditor's report, board's report and annexures, and for listed entities the corporate governance report, management discussion and analysis and business responsibility and sustainability report (top 1,000) under LODR. It is sent to members at least 21 days before the AGM and may be sent electronically. Under s.136 members may also obtain copies and inspect at the registered office.

ICSI's Secretarial Standard on Board's Report (SS-4) was issued as a recommendatory standard to standardise the content and presentation of the report. It suggests a structured format, disclosure of material events and the signing procedure. Though not mandatory, it is useful guidance for drafting.

quiz.q: Annual return must be filed with ROC within:
quiz.explain: Section 92(4) requires filing within 60 days from the date of the AGM.

quiz.q: A private company with turnover of ₹70 crore files its annual return. Certification by a practising CS in MGT-8 is:
quiz.explain: Rule 11(2) requires MGT-8 certification for companies with turnover of ₹50 crore or more.

quiz.q: Which document is NOT part of the board's report under s.134?
options: Statement on declarations by independent directors
quiz.explain: A prospectus is an offer document, not a board's report matter.

quiz.q: Board's report must be signed by:
options: The chairperson if authorised, or at least two directors one of whom is MD
quiz.explain: Section 134(6) prescribes the signing requirement.

quiz.q: A small company may prepare its board's report in:
quiz.explain: Rule 8A provides an abridged board's report for OPCs and small companies.

quiz.q: Annual report must be sent to members at least:
quiz.explain: Section 136(1) requires copies to be sent not less than 21 days before the meeting.

desc.q: The auditor of Rho Ltd has qualified the accounts on non-provision of doubtful debts and reported a fraud below ₹1 crore to the audit committee. As CS, explain how the board's report should deal with these matters, along with its approval and filing.
points: Under s.134(3)(f) the board must give explanations or comments on every qualification, reservation or adverse remark by the auditor.
Details of frauds reported by auditors under s.143(12) (other than those reported to Central Government) must be disclosed under s.134(3)(ca).
Include other mandatory disclosures: meetings held, directors' responsibility statement, RPTs in AOC-2, CSR report, and web link of annual return.
Approve at a board meeting (s.179(3)) and sign as per s.134(6).
Attach to financial statements filed in AOC-4 within 30 days of AGM and send to members 21 days before AGM.

notes.note: Key Managerial Personnel under s.2(51) are the CEO or MD or manager, the CS, the WTD, the CFO, other officers up to one level below directors who are whole-time and designated by the board, and others prescribed. Under s.203 and rule 8, listed companies and public companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more must appoint whole-time KMP, by board resolution, with terms and remuneration; a vacancy must be filled within six months. Private companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more must appoint a whole-time CS (rule 8A).

An MD (s.2(54)) has substantial powers of management, and a WTD (s.2(94)) is a director in whole-time employment. Appointment under s.196 is for a term of up to five years, with age limits of 21 to 70 years (beyond 70 needs a special resolution) and the conditions in Schedule V Part I; the appointment is approved by the board and members and filed in MR-1 within 60 days. A company cannot have both an MD and a manager at the same time, and a person may be MD of at most two companies with unanimous board consent under s.203(3).

A Company Secretary (s.2(24)) is a member of ICSI appointed to perform secretarial functions, and is a KMP and an officer in default. Under s.205 the CS reports to the board on compliance, ensures adherence to secretarial standards and discharges prescribed duties, while under LODR the CS acts as compliance officer of a listed entity. A whole-time CS cannot hold office in more than one company except in its subsidiary.

Section 2(60) lists officers liable for defaults: whole-time directors, KMP, any person specified by the board, persons on whose advice the board acts, any director aware of a contravention through board proceedings who did not object, and share transfer agents for issue or transfer of shares. In the absence of KMP, all directors may be liable. This is key in deciding who bears penalty for a filing failure.

Under s.197 total managerial remuneration of a public company cannot exceed 11% of net profits (computed per s.198), with individual limits of 5% for one MD/WTD/manager, 10% for all of them, and 1% (or 3% without an MD/WTD) for non-executive directors, exceedable with a special resolution. In case of inadequate or no profits, remuneration is governed by Schedule V Part II with limits based on effective capital, or higher with a special resolution. Sitting fees cannot exceed ₹1 lakh per meeting, and excess remuneration must be refunded, held in trust till recovery.

quiz.q: A public company proposes to appoint a 72-year-old person as MD. It needs:
options: Special resolution with justification in the explanatory statement
quiz.explain: Section 196(3)(a) allows appointment beyond 70 years with a special resolution.

quiz.q: The CFO of a listed company resigns on 1 April. The vacancy must be filled by:
quiz.explain: Section 203(4) requires filling the vacancy within six months.

quiz.q: The overall managerial remuneration limit for a public company (without special resolution) is:
quiz.explain: Section 197(1) caps total remuneration at 11% of net profits computed under s.198.

quiz.q: The maximum sitting fee per board meeting payable to a director is:
quiz.explain: Rule 4 of the Managerial Remuneration Rules caps sitting fees at ₹1 lakh per meeting.

quiz.q: A company fails to file AOC-4. It has no KMP and the board has specified no one. Who is the officer in default?
quiz.explain: Section 2(60) provides that where no KMP or specified person exists, all directors are officers in default.

quiz.q: A person is already MD of one company. He can become MD of a second company if:
options: The board approves by unanimous consent at a meeting
quiz.explain: Section 203(3) proviso permits MD of another company with unanimous board consent at a meeting.

desc.q: Sigma Ltd (public, unlisted) has made a loss this year but wants to pay its new WTD remuneration of ₹1.5 crore per annum. Its effective capital is ₹80 crore. Advise.
points: Where profits are inadequate or nil, remuneration is governed by s.197(3) read with Schedule V Part II.

For effective capital between ₹5 crore and ₹100 crore, the Schedule V yearly limit is ₹84 lakh, which may be doubled to ₹1.68 crore by special resolution; ₹1.5 crore exceeds the base limit but is within the doubled limit, so a special resolution is required.
Conditions: board approval with NRC recommendation, no default in repayment of debts or obtain lenders' prior approval, and a statement with information under Schedule V in the notice.
Appointment for term up to 5 years under s.196, with MR-1 filed within 60 days.
Excess remuneration paid without approvals must be refunded and held in trust for the company.
